rows.title: Humdrum: A Short History
pages: Humdrum was laid out in the year the railway didn't come. The surveyors had promised a station; they sent a letter instead.
The town took it well. It built a bandstand where the station would have been, and has held a fair there every spring since.
Nothing of note has happened in Humdrum since. The town council would like that to stay true.

rows.title: Soups for Cold Days
pages: A good soup wants three things: something green, something that grew underground, and time.
In the woods, wild onion and a handful of mushrooms will do for the first two. A camp fire will do for the third.
Stir it, wait, and eat it while it is too hot. That is the whole secret.

rows.title: The Rose and the Hip
pages: After the wild rose flowers, it leaves a small red fruit called a hip. Birds love them. So did your grandmother.
Steeped in hot water, a few hips make a sharp, sweet tea that warms you to the toes on a cold trail.

rows.title: A Walker's Pocket
pages: Never set out without something in your pocket to eat. Berries and hazelnuts, mixed, keep for days and weigh nothing.
The author once walked forty miles on a pocket of trail mix and a stubborn mood. Neither is recommended alone.

rows.title: Knots and Cords
pages: Reeds from the shallows, twisted and plied, make a rope good enough for most jobs a ranger has.
A bowline will hold a load and still come undone when you ask it to. Learn that one first.

rows.title: Reading the Weather
pages: Fog in the morning burns off by noon more often than not. Fog at dusk means a cold night.
When the wind backs round to the north and the birds go quiet, look for shelter before you look for anything else.
Snow is not dangerous. Being wet in the snow is.

rows.title: The Old Road
pages: Before the park had a gate, a cart road ran from Humdrum into the hills. Bits of it still show, if you know where to look.
Most of it is under brush now. The council voted twice to clear it, and twice voted to think about it some more.

rows.title: Birds of the Valley
pages: The heron stands in the shallows for hours and catches more than any angler.
Crows remember faces. Be kind to them.
If you hear an owl at noon, write it down. Somebody at the library will want to know.

rows.title: On Sleeping Out
pages: A bedroll on the ground beats a bed you can't reach before dark.
Keep your boots inside the bedroll on a frosty night. You will thank yourself in the morning.
A fire is company. Put it out before you sleep all the same.

rows.title: The Humdrum Fair, Every Spring
pages: The fair began as a way to use up a bandstand. It became the town's favourite day of the year.
There are pies, a band of uncertain size, and a contest for the largest radish that nobody under eighty has ever won.

rows.title: The town archive
pages: Minutes of the Humdrum Council, spring of the founding year: 'Resolved, that the bandstand be built where the station would have been, so that the town has somewhere to wait.'
A letter, undated: 'Dear Council, the lamps on Main Street are too bright and the moths are complaining. Yours, a resident.' Underneath, in another hand: 'Noted.'
A hand-drawn map of the park gate, with the road marked 'to the ranger' in pencil and a small star beside the station.
A list headed 'Things that have happened in Humdrum', in the mayor's handwriting. It is blank. At the bottom: 'Long may it stay so.'
